withdrawal: 250 m³/h · 55 = 13,750 €/a
injection: 250 m³/h · 55 = 13,750 €/a
total = 77,500 €/a

Product 2 (working gas 0.0475 €/m³/a, rates 60 €/m³/h/a each):
working gas: 1,000,000 · 0.0475 = 47,500 €/a
withdrawal: 250 · 60 = 15,000 €/a
injection: 250 · 60 = 15,000 €/a
total = 77,500 €/a

Both cost 77,500 €/a. Product 2 looks 5 % cheaper on the headline working gas price and is 9 % dearer on both rates; the two effects cancel exactly.

The lesson: a storage price is a vector of three numbers, not one number, so no single component allows a comparison, and a seller can make his offer look cheap on whichever component the buyer happens to look at. Only the total annual charge T_storage, evaluated for the capacities the buyer actually intends to book, is comparable. The next slide adds the second half of the trap: even the total can be equal while the products are worth completely different amounts.

prompt: 'Ambiguity of storage prices II': both products again cost 77,500 €/a, but product 2 has twice the rates and half the cycling time. Verify the total, calculate the two reference prices given in the table, and decide which product a trader should take.
solution:
Product 1: 1,000,000 m³ at 0.05 €/m³/a = 50,000 €/a; withdrawal 250 m³/h at 55 = 13,750 €/a; injection 250 m³/h at 55 = 13,750 €/a; total 77,500 €/a; cycling time 8,000 h.
Product 2: 1,000,000 m³ at 0.025 €/m³/a = 25,000 €/a; withdrawal 500 m³/h at 52.50 = 26,250 €/a; injection 500 m³/h at 52.50 = 26,250 €/a; total 77,500 €/a; cycling time 4,000 h.

Reference price per unit of working gas:
energy = 1,000,000 m³ · 11 kWh/m³ = 11,000,000 kWh = 11,000 MWh
77,500 € / 11,000 MWh = 7.05 €/MWh/a — identical for both products.

Reference price per unit of withdrawal rate:
Product 1: 77,500 / 250 m³/h = 310 €/(m³/h)/a; in power terms 250 · 11 = 2,750 kW, so 77,500 / 2,750 = 28.18 €/kW/a.
Product 2: 77,500 / 500 m³/h = 155 €/(m³/h)/a; 500 · 11 = 5,500 kW, so 77,500 / 5,500 = 14.09 €/kW/a.

So measured per MWh of working gas the two products are exactly equally expensive, while measured per kW of withdrawal rate product 2 is half the price. Which is 'cheaper' depends entirely on the reference unit — that is the ambiguity.

Decision: product 2 dominates. It costs the same, offers the same inventory and twice the rates, and its cycling time of 4,000 h instead of 8,000 h means it can be turned over twice in a storage year instead of once. If the trader really cycles twice, his specific storage cost falls to 77,500 / 22,000 MWh = 3.52 €/MWh, so he breaks even at half the summer/winter spread. Product 1 is only equivalent for a trader who has a purely seasonal strategy and will never use the extra rate — and even then the extra rate is free optionality, i.e. extrinsic value.

prompt: The number of hours a storage product needs to fill and to empty its working gas volume once at the contracted rates is called the ___.
solution: The cycling time (cycling period). For product 1 of the slide: 1,000,000 m³ / 250 m³/h = 4,000 h to fill plus 4,000 h to empty = 8,000 h. Product 2 has twice the rates and therefore a cycling time of 4,000 h, so it can be turned over twice in a storage year. Since a year has 8,760 h, the cycling time translates directly into the number of cycles — and thus into how many times the annual charge can be earned back from a price spread.

prompt: Explain the 'merit order' of German storages. What is on the axes, what does the curve look like, and how do you use it together with the summer/winter spread? Convert the horizontal axis into energy as a cross-check.
solution:
Axes: the horizontal axis is the cumulated working gas capacity of the German storage facilities in million m³, running to about 21,000 mio. m³; the vertical axis is the specific cost of that capacity in €/MWh of working gas. The facilities are sorted by rising specific cost, exactly like power plants in an electricity merit order.

Shape: a rising staircase. It starts at about 3.7 €/MWh, sits on a broad plateau around 4.3 €/MWh up to roughly 5,000 mio. m³, steps to about 4.8 and then to about 6.6 €/MWh at around 9,000 mio. m³, climbs slowly to about 8 €/MWh at 16,000 mio. m³ and ends steeply at about 10.8 €/MWh. Each step is one facility or one product; the cheap left end is the large, slow pore storages, the expensive right end the fast caverns and small facilities.

Use: the summer/winter spread plays the role of the market price. A storage is worth booking only if its specific cost lies below the spread, because the profitability condition is p_supply + p_storage < p_sales. Draw a horizontal line at the spread and everything to the left of the intersection is in the money. At a spread of 5 €/MWh only roughly 8,000 to 9,000 mio. m³, i.e. about 40 % of German working gas capacity, covers its cost; at 8 €/MWh it is about 16,000 mio. m³, i.e. some 75 %. This is why the thin spreads of recent years left part of the German capacity commercially unbookable — and why filling obligations had to replace the market signal.

Cross-check of the axis: 21,000 mio. m³ · 11 kWh/m³ = 231,000 GWh = 231 TWh, which fits the German working gas capacity of about 245 to 260 TWh reported in the GIE table earlier in the chapter.
